lead: break, continue and pass are three small keywords that change how a loop runs. break leaves the loop at once. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one. pass does nothing. They exist so a program can stop early, skip unwanted items, or keep a block legal while it is still empty. Search loops, input checks and function stubs use them daily. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic.

sections.h3: break and continue: leaving versus skipping

blocks.text: break stops the nearest loop that contains it. Control jumps to the first line after the loop; the condition is not tested again and a for takes no more items. Use it when further work is useless: in a search for a roll number, once the number is found, break saves the remaining comparisons. Inside nested loops, break leaves only the inner loop. The outer loop continues. To leave both, use a flag or return from a function.

continue ends only the current iteration. In a for, Python takes the next item. In a while, Python jumps to the condition test. Code after continue in the same block is skipped. If the increment is after continue, a while may loop forever.

The difference is scope. break exits the loop; continue exits one iteration. Example: for i in range(1, 7): if i == 3: continue; print(i) prints 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6. Only 3 is skipped. Change continue to break and the output stops at 1 and 2.

pass does nothing. Python needs at least one statement in every indented block after if, for, while, def or class. When the real code is not written yet, pass keeps the block legal. A stub like def pay(): pass can be imported, called and tested before its body exists.

pass is not break and not continue. It does not skip the rest of an iteration and does not leave a loop. It simply lets the program move to the next statement. Removing it from an empty block gives IndentationError: expected an indented block.
Use pass for an unfinished branch, an empty function or class stub, or a deliberate no-op. It has no effect on loop control. In an exam, write pass when a block must exist but no action is defined.

figure.caption: The loop prints 1, 2, 3 and 5. The continue path skips only i = 4; break at i = 6 ends the loop.

spec.title: break and continue in a for loop
spec.aria: Flowchart for i from 1 to 6: i = 4 takes the continue path that skips printing, i = 6 takes break, so printed values are 1, 2, 3, 5.

examples.question: Trace this program and give its output, one value per line: for i in range(1, 7): if i == 4: continue; if i == 6: break; print(i).
examples.answer: Output: 1, 2, 3 and 5, each on its own line.

traps: continue before the increment in a while loop can cause an infinite loop; update the variable before continue.
break exits only the innermost loop. In nested loops, the outer loop still runs.
pass is not a skip; it does nothing, so the rest of the block and the loop continue normally.
A break inside an if still breaks the enclosing loop; the if is not a loop.

quiz.q: Which keyword leaves the nearest loop immediately?

quiz.a: break exits the loop; continue exits only the current iteration.

quiz.q: What does this print? for i in range(1,6): if i % 2 == 0: continue; print(i)

quiz.a: At i = 1, continue jumps back to the condition test before i += 1 runs, so i stays 1 forever.

quiz.q: In for i in range(1,7): if i==4: continue; if i==6: break; print(i), what is printed?
A nested loop has break inside the inner loop. Which loops stop?
quiz.a: Only the inner loop stops; the outer loop continues.

beyond: Not for the exam. Python's for...else and while...else run an else block when the loop ends without break; search for 'loop else Python' to see the pattern. Code checkers flag pass as unfinished work, so production stubs often raise NotImplementedError instead. In parsers and search tools, break and continue are still the fast way to prune work. Search next for 'guard clause' and 'loop else'.
